items.prompt: Which keyword makes one Java class inherit from another class?

options.label: `inherits`
`extends`
`super`
`implements`

rubric: `extends` declares class inheritance.
`implements` is for interfaces, and `inherits` is not a Java keyword.

items.prompt: Which method signature is the standard entry point the JVM looks for when starting a Java program?

options.label: `public void main(String[] args)`
`static int main(String[] args)`
`public static void main(String[] args)`
`public static main(String args)`

rubric: The entry point must be public, static, void and take a String array.
Distractors drop `static`, change the return type, or use the wrong parameter type.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a primitive type in Java?

options.label: `String`
`int`
`double`
`boolean`

rubric: `String` is a class, so it is a reference type.
Learners often treat `String` as primitive because string literals are so common.

items.prompt: Which collection interface is defined to hold no duplicate elements?

options.label: `List`
`ArrayList`
`Set`
`Deque`

rubric: A `Set` forbids duplicates.
`List` and `Deque` allow duplicates, and `ArrayList` is a concrete List class.

items.prompt: Which keyword is used inside a method body to raise an exception object?

options.label: `raise`
`throw`
`throws`
`catch`

rubric: `throw` raises an exception.
`throws` only declares in a method signature that exceptions may escape.

items.prompt: Which of these are checked exceptions in Java, meaning the compiler forces you to catch or declare them? Select all that apply.

options.label: `NullPointerException`
`ClassNotFoundException`
`IOException`
`IllegalArgumentException`

rubric: `IOException` and `ClassNotFoundException` are checked.
The other two extend `RuntimeException` and are unchecked.

items.prompt: A learner has saved a file named `Hello.java` containing a valid class. They open a terminal in the same folder and want to compile the source into bytecode with the JDK. Which command does this?

options.label: `javac Hello.java`
`java Hello.class`
`javadoc Hello.java`
`jar Hello.java`

rubric: `javac` is the Java compiler and produces `.class` bytecode.
`java` runs compiled classes, `jar` packages archives, and `javadoc` makes documentation.

items.prompt: Two variables `a` and `b` each refer to a different `String` object created with `new String("hi")`. What does `a == b` evaluate to, and why?

options.label: `false`, because strings can never be compared with `==`
`true`, because both strings have the same length
`true`, because both strings contain the same characters
`false`, because `==` compares references, not contents

rubric: `==` on objects tests whether they are the same object; `equals` compares contents.
Distractors assume `==` compares contents or that it cannot be used on strings.

items.prompt: What value does `int x = 7 / 2;` store in `x`?
rubric: Integer division truncates the fractional part, giving 3.
`3.5` ignores integer division, and `4` assumes rounding.

items.prompt: Why would a programmer declare `List<String> names` instead of a raw `List names`?

options.label: The list can only be used inside a single method of that class
The compiler checks element types, so wrong types are caught early
The list becomes immutable, so elements cannot be changed later
The list runs faster because strings are stored as primitives

rubric: Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts.
Distractors credit generics with performance, immutability or scope effects they do not have.

items.prompt: How does the JVM make compiled Java programs portable across operating systems?

options.label: The compiler produces separate native executables for each OS
Source code is re-parsed by each OS's own text editor
Programs are converted to C code that every OS can compile
Bytecode runs on a JVM built for each platform

rubric: Bytecode is platform-neutral and each platform's JVM executes it.
Distractors imagine per-OS native builds or translation to C.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how Java classes relate to interfaces and superclasses?

options.label: A class may extend many classes but implement one interface
A class may extend many classes and implement many interfaces
A class may extend one class and implement no interfaces
A class may extend one class and implement many interfaces

rubric: Java allows single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation.
Distractors reverse the rule or assume multiple class inheritance.

items.prompt: Which statements about a `try`-with-resources statement are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It works only with classes from the `java.io` package
Resources implementing `AutoCloseable` are closed automatically
A `finally` block is required to close the resource
Resources are closed even if the try body throws an exception

rubric: It closes `AutoCloseable` resources automatically, including on exceptions.
A `finally` block is not required, and any `AutoCloseable` works, not just I/O classes.

items.prompt: A student runs this code: `Set<Integer> s = new HashSet<>(); s.add(5); s.add(5); s.add(6); System.out.println(s.size());` They expected the output to be 3 because three `add` calls were made. What is actually printed?
rubric: A `HashSet` ignores the duplicate 5, leaving two elements.
The expected 3 assumes every `add` call stores a new element, as a `List` would.

items.prompt: Two Strings are created with `new String("java")` and stored in `a` and `b`. How do `a == b` and `a.equals(b)` differ?

options.label: `==` compares the characters, while `equals` compares memory addresses
`==` compares object references, while `equals` compares the characters
`==` ignores letter case, while `equals` requires exact characters
`==` works only on primitives, so on Strings it always throws an error

rubric: `==` tests whether both variables point to the same object; `equals` compares content.
Distractors reverse the two meanings or invent case rules.

items.prompt: Why can a Java class implement several interfaces but extend only one superclass?

options.label: Interfaces are compiled faster, so the JVM permits more of them per class
Interfaces are only documentation, so the compiler ignores them when linking
Superclasses are limited because every class already extends `Object` once per file
Interfaces carry no instance state, which avoids the ambiguity of inheriting fields from many parents

rubric: Java restricts class inheritance to one parent to avoid conflicting state; interfaces don't hold instance fields.
Distractors give false technical reasons about speed or `Object`.

items.prompt: Which of these is a checked exception that the compiler forces you to catch or declare?

options.label: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`
`NullPointerException`
`IllegalArgumentException`
`IOException`

rubric: `IOException` extends `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`, so it is checked.
The others are runtime (unchecked) exceptions.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of declaring `List<String> names` instead of a raw `List names`?

options.label: The list sorts itself alphabetically because the element type is known
The compiler rejects adding non-String elements and removes the need for casts when reading
The list becomes immutable once the type is given in angle brackets
The list then stores its strings in less memory at runtime

rubric: Generics give compile-time type checking and avoid casts.
Distractors attribute memory, immutability or sorting effects to generics.

items.prompt: What does it mean that Java is described as "write once, run anywhere"?

options.label: Source code is translated by the JVM into C before every single run
Source code is compiled to native machine code that works on every CPU
Source code is compiled to bytecode that any installed JVM can execute
Source code is interpreted line by line directly by the operating system

rubric: javac produces platform-neutral bytecode that a JVM on each platform runs.
Distractors confuse bytecode with native code or OS interpretation.

items.prompt: Which of these standard collection types reject duplicate elements? Select all that apply.

options.label: `HashSet`
`TreeSet`
`ArrayDeque`
`ArrayList`

rubric: Set implementations such as `HashSet` and `TreeSet` keep only unique elements.
`ArrayList` and `ArrayDeque` allow duplicates.

items.prompt: A teammate writes `new FileReader("data.txt")` inside `main` and gets the compile error: "unreported exception FileNotFoundException; must be caught or declared to be thrown". What does this error tell them?

options.label: It is a checked exception, so they must add try/catch or a `throws` clause
An import for `FileReader` is missing, so the class can't be found
The file is missing at runtime, so they must create `data.txt` first
The exception is unchecked, so it must be wrapped in a `RuntimeException`

rubric: Checked exceptions must be handled or declared at compile time.
Distractors confuse compile-time and runtime problems or blame imports.

items.prompt:
What does this code print?
`int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; int s = 0; for (int x : a) { s += x * x; } System.out.println(s);`
rubric: 6 is the plain sum; others are arithmetic slips.

items.prompt:
What does this code print?
`String s = "hi"; s.concat(" there"); System.out.println(s);`

options.label: null
hi there
hi
there

rubric: Strings are immutable; `concat` returns a new String that was discarded.
"hi there" assumes the original is modified.

items.prompt:
What does this code print?
`Map<String,Integer> m = new HashMap<>(); m.put("a", 1); m.put("a", 2); System.out.println(m.size() + " " + m.get("a"));`
rubric: Putting an existing key replaces its value, so size is 1 and value 2.
Distractors assume duplicate keys or keeping the first value.

items.prompt:
What does this statement print?
`System.out.println(7 / 2 + 7 % 2);`
rubric: 7/2 is integer division = 3, 7%2 = 1, total 4.
4.5 assumes floating-point division.

items.prompt:
What is printed?
`try { System.out.print("A"); throw new RuntimeException(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.print("B"); } finally { System.out.print("C"); } System.out.print("D");`

options.label: ABCD
ABD
ACD
ABC

rubric: The exception is caught, finally always runs, then execution continues with D.
Distractors skip finally or the code after the block.

items.prompt: Which of these declarations compile without error? Select all that apply.

options.label: `List<String> l = new ArrayList<Integer>();`
`Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();`
`Object o = "text";`
`List<int> nums = new ArrayList<>();`
`List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();`

rubric: Generics require reference types, and the type arguments must match; any String is an Object.
`List<int>` and mismatched type arguments do not compile.

items.prompt: A class `Animal` has `String speak() { return "..."; }`. `Dog extends Animal` overrides it to return "Woof". In `main` you write `Animal a = new Dog(); System.out.println(a.speak());`. What is printed?

options.label: null
A compile error, because `Animal` cannot refer to a `Dog`
Woof

rubric: Overridden methods are chosen by the runtime object type (dynamic dispatch).
"..." assumes the declared type decides which method runs.

items.prompt:
What does this code print?
`Map<String,Integer> m = new TreeMap<>();`
`for (String s : "b a b c a b".split(" ")) m.merge(s, 1, Integer::sum);`
`System.out.println(m);`
rubric: merge adds 1 per occurrence and TreeMap sorts keys, giving {a=2, b=3, c=1}.
{b=3, a=2, c=1} assumes insertion order, which a TreeMap does not keep.

items.prompt: Given `static int f() { try { return 1; } finally { System.out.print("F"); } }`, what is printed by `System.out.print(f());`?

options.label: F1
F
1F

rubric: The finally block runs before the method returns to the caller, so F prints first and then the caller prints 1.
1F assumes the return value is printed before finally runs.

items.prompt:
What does this print?
`Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 1000, d = 1000;`
`System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d));`

options.label: true true
false true
true false
false false

rubric: Autoboxing caches Integer values from -128 to 127, so a == b compares the same object while c == d compares two distinct objects.
true true assumes == compares values for all boxed Integers.

items.prompt: You need one method that sums the elements of a `List<Integer>` and also of a `List<Double>`, returning a double. Which signature lets both calls compile?

options.label: `double sum(List<? super Number> xs)`
`double sum(List<Object> xs)`
`double sum(List<Number> xs)`
`double sum(List<? extends Number> xs)`

rubric: An upper-bounded wildcard accepts List of any Number subtype, and its elements can be read as Number.
List<Number> is not a supertype of List<Integer> because generics are invariant.

items.prompt:
What does this code print?
`String s = "ab";`
`s.concat("c");`
`s += "d";`
`System.out.println(s);`

options.label: abd
ab
abcabd
abcd

rubric: Strings are immutable, so the result of concat is discarded; only += reassigns s, giving abd.
abcd assumes concat modifies s in place.

items.prompt: Given `List<Integer> list = List.of(1, 2, 3);`, which calls throw `UnsupportedOperationException` at run time? Select all that apply.

options.label: `list.add(4)`
`list.get(0)`
`list.remove(0)`
`list.set(0, 9)`
`list.contains(2)`

rubric: List.of returns an immutable list, so every mutating method (add, set, remove) throws.
get and contains only read, so they work normally.

items.prompt: A payroll report must list employees by department A to Z, and within each department by highest salary first. `Employee` is a record with `dept()` (String) and `salary()` (double). Which comparator produces this order?

options.label: `Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary)`
`Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())`
`Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary).reversed()`
`Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).thenComparing(Employee::dept)`

rubric: Only the salary key is reversed, via the reverseOrder comparator passed to thenComparing.
Calling reversed() at the end reverses the whole chain, including department order.

items.prompt: The loop `for (String s : names) { if (s.isEmpty()) names.remove(s); }` over an `ArrayList` sometimes throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. What is the cause?

options.label: `isEmpty()` takes a lock on the string that the list then cannot release
The list's modification count changes outside the iterator, so the iterator's next call fails fast
`remove(Object)` is not permitted on an ArrayList while it is non-empty
The for-each loop iterates over a copy, which goes stale after a removal

rubric: ArrayList's iterator compares a modification count and fails fast when the list changes without using the iterator.
The copy explanation is wrong: for-each iterates the live list.

items.prompt: A class `Point` overrides `equals(Object)` to compare x and y but not `hashCode()`. After `set.add(new Point(1,2))` on a `HashSet`, `set.contains(new Point(1,2))` usually returns false. Why?

options.label: HashSet rejects classes that override equals without implementing Comparable
contains calls hashCode on the set itself, which has changed after the add
HashSet compares elements with == and only uses equals when sizes differ
The default hashCode usually sends the two equal points to different buckets, so equals is never called

rubric: HashSet locates a bucket by hashCode first; equal objects must have equal hash codes or lookups miss.
The == explanation ignores that HashSet does call equals within a bucket.

items.prompt: A class declares both `void process(List<String> a)` and `void process(List<Integer> a)`. It fails to compile with a name clash. What is the underlying reason?

options.label: Overloading is only allowed when return types differ, and both return void here
The compiler cannot tell Integer from String because both implement Comparable
Generic methods may not be overloaded in a class that also has a main method
Both parameter types erase to `List`, so the two methods have the same signature after erasure

rubric: Type erasure removes the type arguments, so both signatures become process(List), a duplicate.
Overloading depends on parameter types, never on return type alone.

items.prompt: `class A { String n = "A"; String get() { return n; } }` and `class B extends A { String n = "B"; }`. Why does `new B().get()` return "A"?

options.label: Fields are not overridden; B's n only hides A's, and get() in A refers to A's n
B's constructor never runs, so its field n is left unset
Methods not marked final are bound at compile time, so get() reads A's field
B's n is private by default, so inherited methods cannot see it

rubric: Field access is resolved by the static type of the declaring code, so there is no polymorphism for fields.
Non-final methods are bound at run time, so the compile-time binding claim is wrong.

items.prompt: `List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(); IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel().forEach(out::add);` sometimes ends with fewer than 1000 elements or throws an exception. What is the cause?

options.label: `forEach` on a parallel stream runs on one thread, which overflows the array
`range` produces duplicate values when run in parallel, so some adds are dropped
ArrayList is not thread-safe, so concurrent adds from several threads corrupt its state
Autoboxing of ints is not allowed on worker threads, so some values are lost

rubric: Parallel forEach calls add from multiple threads on an unsynchronised ArrayList, causing lost updates or index errors.
The fix is to use collect(Collectors.toList()) or a thread-safe collection.

items.prompt: A method catches `Exception e` and throws `new RuntimeException("failed")`; in production the root cause cannot be found. Which changes preserve the information needed to diagnose it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Throw `new RuntimeException("failed", e)` so the original is the cause
Catch `Throwable` instead of `Exception` and keep the same throw
Log the throwable itself, with its stack trace, before throwing
Log only `e.getMessage()` and then throw the same exception
Call `e.fillInStackTrace()` before discarding e

rubric: Chaining the cause or logging the full throwable keeps the original stack trace.
getMessage alone loses the trace, and fillInStackTrace actually resets it.

items.prompt: A service keeps `static Map<Long, Session> cache = new HashMap<>();` and adds a Session per login but never removes any. After several days it fails with `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. A heap dump shows millions of Session objects. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The young generation is too small, so objects are promoted early and never collected
The static map strongly references every Session, so the GC can never reclaim them
The GC skips objects that were created while a static method was running
Session objects define no finalizer, so the GC cannot reclaim them

rubric: Objects reachable from a static strong reference are never collected, so the map grows without bound; fix with eviction or weak references.
Finalizers are not required for collection, and being created in a static method does not exempt an object.

items.prompt: Given `class Base { Base() { init(); } void init() {} }` and `class Sub extends Base { private String name = "ready"; @Override void init() { System.out.println(name); } }`, what does `new Sub()` print?

options.label: `null`, because Sub's field initialisers run only after Base's constructor has finished
A `NullPointerException`, because `name` cannot be read during construction
`ready`, because the field initialiser runs before any constructor body executes
`ready`, because overriding methods are bound only once construction completes

rubric: The Base constructor runs first and calls the overridden init() before Sub's field initialisers run, so name is still null.
Distractors assume initialisers run first or that dispatch is deferred during construction.

items.prompt: A list `["a","b","c"]` is an `ArrayList<String>` iterated with a for-each loop that calls `list.remove(...)` on the current element. Which removal completes the loop without a `ConcurrentModificationException`?

options.label: Removing `"c"` when visited, because no later element remains to be iterated over
Removing `"a"` when visited, because the iterator then resynchronises with the shifted list
None; every structural change during iteration is detected by the next call to next()
Removing `"b"` when visited, because hasNext() then finds the cursor equal to the new size

rubric: After removing the second-to-last element, cursor equals size, so hasNext() returns false and no check occurs.
Removing the last element leaves cursor != size, so next() throws; people wrongly think the last element is safe.

items.prompt: The code `List<? extends Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>(); nums.add(Integer.valueOf(1));` fails to compile. What is the actual reason?

options.label: Wildcard-typed lists are read-only views, so every mutator method is blocked by the compiler
`Integer` does not extend `Number`, so the argument type is incompatible with the list
The element type is unknown to the compiler, so only `null` can be added type-safely
`Number` is abstract, so no instance of it can ever be added to such a list

rubric: With an upper-bounded wildcard the compiler cannot prove the list accepts Integer (it could be List<Double>), so only null is allowed.
Distractors confuse this with abstractness or claim all mutators are blocked, though remove and clear compile.

items.prompt: Consider `static int f() { try { throw new IllegalStateException(); } finally { return 1; } }`. What happens when `f()` is called?

options.label: It does not compile, because a try block without catch cannot have a finally that returns
It returns 1; the return in finally silently discards the pending exception
It throws `IllegalStateException`, because finally runs first and then the exception propagates
It returns 1, and the JVM prints the discarded exception to stderr before returning

rubric: A return in finally overrides the abrupt completion of try, so the exception is lost without any trace.
Distractors assume the exception always propagates or is logged automatically.

items.prompt: `List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(); IntStream.range(0, 10000).parallel().forEach(out::add);` sometimes leaves `out` with fewer than 10000 elements or throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. What is the cause?

options.label: `IntStream.range` is exclusive of the upper bound, so a varying number of values go missing
`ArrayList` is not thread-safe, so concurrent add calls corrupt its size counter and backing array
`parallel()` reorders elements, and some values are dropped when the stream is split between threads
Autoboxing in `out::add` creates duplicate Integer objects that the list then rejects as repeated

rubric: Parallel forEach calls add from several threads on an unsynchronised ArrayList, causing lost updates and resize races.
Distractors blame ordering, boxing or range bounds, none of which drop elements.

items.prompt: A `HashSet<Point>` returns false from `contains(p)` for a point `p` that equals one added earlier. Which of these could explain it? Select all that apply.

options.label: `hashCode` returns the constant 1 for every point, so lookups skip the correct bucket
`equals` compares x and y while `hashCode` uses only x, so lookups land in wrong buckets
`hashCode` uses a field that was modified after the point was added to the set
`equals` is overridden but `hashCode` is not, so equal points hash to different buckets

rubric: Missing hashCode override or a mutated hash field puts the lookup in a different bucket than the stored entry.
A constant hash or a hash on a subset of equals' fields stays consistent; it only hurts speed.

items.prompt: A long-running service caches computed reports in a `static Map<RequestKey, Report>` and never removes entries. Over days, old-generation usage after each full GC climbs until `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. A heap dump shows millions of `RequestKey` objects. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Finalizers run too slowly, so unreachable keys pile up before the collector can reclaim them
The maximum heap is configured too low, so garbage collection cannot run effectively at all
Entries remain strongly reachable from a static field, so the collector can never reclaim them
Metaspace is exhausted by loaded classes, which crowds out heap space for newly created objects

rubric: Objects reachable from a static map are live, so GC cannot free them; this is a logical leak.
Distractors blame finalizers, heap sizing or metaspace, but usage that keeps growing after full GCs points to retained live objects.

items.prompt: You must deduplicate incoming IDs, iterate them in first-seen order, and get O(1) average-time `contains`. Sorted order is not needed. Which choice best meets all criteria?

options.label: `HashSet`, since hashed lookup is fast and iteration follows first-seen order
`TreeSet`, since iteration is ordered and logarithmic `contains` is fast enough anyway
`LinkedHashSet`, since hashed lookup is retained and iteration follows insertion order
`ArrayList`, since it preserves order and `contains` scans in constant time

rubric: LinkedHashSet combines hash-based contains with insertion-ordered iteration.
HashSet gives no order guarantee, TreeSet sorts rather than preserving arrival order, and ArrayList.contains is linear.

items.prompt: You design `loadConfig(Path)`. Criteria: callers can plausibly recover from a missing file by using defaults, the API should make them consider that, and programming errors such as a null path should not clutter signatures. Which design is best?

options.label: Checked for both, since the compiler should force every caller to handle every possible failure
Checked exception for a missing file, since callers can recover; unchecked for a null path, since that is a bug
Unchecked for both, since checked exceptions never help callers recover and clutter every signature
Return null for a missing file, since exceptions should be reserved for failures the JVM itself raises

rubric: Checked exceptions suit recoverable conditions callers should handle; unchecked ones suit programming errors.
Distractors apply a single blanket rule or use null returns, which hide the failure.

items.prompt: A metrics counter is incremented by 64 threads millions of times per second and read once per minute. Criteria: maximise write throughput; an exact total at read time is sufficient. Which is best?

options.label: `AtomicLong`, since a single compare-and-swap target gives the best throughput under heavy contention
`LongAdder`, since striped cells reduce contention and `sum()` is acceptable for rare reads
`volatile long` with `++`, since volatile makes the increment both atomic and lock-free
`synchronized` increment, since intrinsic locks scale better than CAS retries under contention

rubric: LongAdder spreads updates across cells, trading a slightly costlier read for much higher write throughput.
AtomicLong suffers CAS contention, volatile ++ is not atomic, and locking is slowest under contention.

items.prompt: You need a set that counts every element ever added, reusing `HashSet`. Criterion: counts must stay correct even if the superclass's internal self-calls change between releases. Which design is best?

options.label: Extend `HashSet` and override only `add`, since every other insertion path is guaranteed to call it
Extend `HashSet` and make the counter static, since shared state stays correct across all subclasses
Wrap a `HashSet` in a forwarding class that counts, since it does not rely on superclass self-calls
Extend `HashSet` and override `add` and `addAll`, since covering every adding method keeps counts correct

rubric: Composition with forwarding isolates the class from implementation details such as addAll calling add (fragile base class).
Overriding add/addAll can double count if addAll calls add internally, and the static counter is simply wrong.

items.prompt: A class keeps a private `List<String> tags`. Criteria: callers cannot modify the list, and a list a caller already holds must never reflect later changes to the class's own list. Which getter body is best?

options.label: `return List.copyOf(tags);` since it is an immutable snapshot taken at call time
`return Collections.unmodifiableList(tags);` since it blocks writes and freezes the visible contents
`return tags;` since a private field behind a getter is already protected from callers
`return new ArrayList<>(tags);` since a detached copy is protected from the internal list

rubric: List.copyOf yields an unmodifiable snapshot, meeting both criteria.
unmodifiableList is a live view that shows later changes; an ArrayList copy is mutable; returning the field exposes it.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to prefer try-with-resources over a manual try/finally that calls `close()`? Select all that apply.

options.label: It works with any class that has a `close()` method, with no interface required
Several resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration
It closes the resource automatically even when the body throws
It guarantees closing even when `System.exit` is called inside the body
Exceptions thrown by `close()` are attached as suppressed, so the primary exception survives

rubric: Automatic closing, suppressed exceptions and reverse-order closing are real advantages over hand-written finally blocks.
System.exit skips the close, and the resource must implement AutoCloseable.

items.prompt: A batch job must process 10,000 CPU-bound tasks on an 8-core server. Criteria: maximise throughput and keep memory bounded; tasks never block on I/O. Which executor setup is best?

options.label: A fixed pool of 1,000 threads, since more threads always finish CPU-bound batches sooner than fewer
A fixed pool of about 8 threads, since extra threads add only context-switching for CPU-bound work
A single-thread executor, since it avoids synchronisation overhead and bounds memory more than any pool
A cached thread pool, since spawning a thread per task maximises parallelism and finishes the batch sooner

rubric: For CPU-bound work, a pool near the core count uses all cores with bounded threads and little overhead.
Cached or very large pools create thousands of threads with memory and switching costs; one thread wastes cores.

items.prompt: A lazy singleton uses `if (inst == null) { synchronized (LOCK) { if (inst == null) inst = new Foo(); } }`, where `inst` is a plain, non-volatile static field. Which critique is correct?

options.label: It is safe, because Java forbids reordering of any write that happens inside a synchronized block, even for readers outside it
It is safe, because the synchronized block makes construction atomic for every thread that later reads the field
It is flawed: a thread passing the unsynchronized first check can see a non-null reference to a partly constructed Foo
It is flawed because two threads can both enter the synchronized block and each create a separate Foo instance

rubric: Without volatile there is no happens-before edge for the unsynchronized read, so a partly constructed object can be observed.
Distractors wrongly assume locking protects readers who never take the lock, or that the inner null check fails.

items.prompt: A worker loop runs `while (true) { try { handle(queue.take()); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("ignored"); } }`. Judged by the need for clean shutdown via interrupt, what is the most serious flaw?

options.label: take() should be replaced by a busy-wait on isEmpty(), because blocking calls cannot respond to interrupts
The catch block swallows the interrupt without restoring the flag or leaving the loop, so the shutdown request is lost
Warn-level logging will flood the logs during normal operation and hide more important errors from operators
InterruptedException is checked, so run() should declare it with throws instead of catching it inside the loop

rubric: Swallowing InterruptedException discards the cancellation signal; the code should restore the flag or exit.
Distractors focus on logging, on an illegal throws clause for Runnable.run, or on a false claim about blocking calls.

items.prompt: Criteria: a utility copies elements from a source list into a destination list; it must accept a `List<Number>` destination with a `List<Integer>` source, and must stop the method from adding to the source. Which signature is best?

options.label: `void copy(List<Number> dst, List<Integer> src)`
`<T> void copy(List<T> dst, List<T> src)`
`<T> void copy(List<? super T> dst, List<? extends T> src)`
`<T> void copy(List<? extends T> dst, List<? super T> src)`

rubric: Producer extends, consumer super: the source produces T (? extends T) and the destination consumes T (? super T).
Distractors reverse the wildcards or fix the types so they are not reusable.

items.prompt: Judged by correctness and expected speedup, which workload is the best candidate for `parallelStream()`?

options.label: Appending every mapped element to a shared ArrayList inside forEach so the result list is built faster
Summing the results of a CPU-heavy, side-effect-free function over a 5-million-element ArrayList
Processing a 20-element list where each step is a trivial arithmetic operation, to cut latency
Calling a blocking HTTP endpoint for each of 200 list elements, relying on the common pool to overlap the waits

rubric: Parallel streams pay off for large, CPU-bound, stateless, easily split work.
Distractors involve blocking I/O on the shared pool, unsafe shared mutation, or overhead that dwarfs tiny workloads.

items.prompt: A method body throws IOException A, then the resource's `close()` throws IOException B. Judge why try-with-resources is preferred over try/finally with a manual `close()` call.

options.label: It silently suppresses every close() failure, so callers only ever see the exception thrown by the body of the method
It propagates A and attaches B with addSuppressed, whereas a finally-based close would let B mask A
It lets B replace A while keeping A as its cause, so callers always see the most recent failure in the chain
It closes the resource before the body completes, so resources are released earlier than they would be in a finally block

rubric: The primary exception is preserved and the close failure is recorded as suppressed, keeping the root cause visible.
Distractors invent silent suppression, exception replacement, or early closing, none of which happens.

items.prompt: Which are sound judgments about iterating collections and ConcurrentModificationException? Select all that apply.

options.label: Fail-fast iterators detect structural modification on a best-effort basis, so program correctness must not depend on the exception being thrown
Iterating a `Collections.synchronizedList` needs no external locking, since each individual method call is synchronized
A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator works on a snapshot, so it does not throw but also does not reflect later changes
A single-threaded loop cannot throw ConcurrentModificationException because only one thread ever touches the list
Calling `iterator.remove()` during traversal is a supported way to delete elements without triggering the exception

rubric: Fail-fast is best-effort, Iterator.remove is supported, and copy-on-write iterators use snapshots.
Distractors claim single-threaded code is immune (removing inside a for-each throws) or that synchronizedList iteration is automatically safe.

items.prompt: A service caches results with `if (!cache.containsKey(k)) { cache.put(k, loadFromDb(k)); }` on a ConcurrentHashMap. Monitoring shows the same key being loaded by several threads at once, causing database spikes. Which change best fixes this while keeping per-key concurrency and simple code?

options.label: Call `cache.putIfAbsent(k, loadFromDb(k))`, because putIfAbsent guarantees the database is queried only once per key
Wrap the cache in `Collections.synchronizedMap`, because then the containsKey and put pair becomes one atomic operation
Use `cache.computeIfAbsent(k, this::loadFromDb)`, so the loader runs atomically per key without a global lock
Make the whole method `synchronized`, so only one thread at a time can touch the cache and the same key is never loaded twice

rubric: computeIfAbsent makes check-and-load atomic per key.
putIfAbsent still evaluates loadFromDb eagerly, and a global lock or synchronized wrapper serializes all keys or leaves the compound action non-atomic.

items.prompt: Design constraints: an in-memory cache holds at most 100 entries, evicts the least recently accessed entry, and keeps O(1) get and put. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Extend `HashMap` and override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > 100`, relying on hash order for eviction
Extend `LinkedHashMap` using its default insertion ordering and override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > 100`, evicting the oldest-inserted entry
Wrap a `TreeMap` keyed by last-access time and remove `firstKey()` whenever the size exceeds 100, re-keying on each access
Extend `LinkedHashMap` with the accessOrder=true constructor and override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > 100`

rubric: LinkedHashMap in access order with removeEldestEntry gives LRU eviction in O(1).
Distractors use a class without that hook, FIFO insertion order, or a TreeMap with O(log n) operations.

items.prompt: Design a method returning the largest element of a non-empty collection. It must compile for `List<java.sql.Timestamp>` (Timestamp extends Date, which implements `Comparable<Date>`) and return the element type. Which signature meets this?

options.label: `<T extends Comparable<T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c)`
`<T> T max(Collection<? super T> c)`
`<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c)`
`<T extends Comparable<? extends T>> T max(Collection<T> c)`

rubric: Comparable<? super T> admits types that inherit their comparison from a supertype, such as Timestamp via Date.
Comparable<T> rejects Timestamp, and the other options either misplace the wildcard or lose the ordering bound.

items.prompt: Design a pipeline with 1 producer and 3 consumers. Constraints: memory use is bounded, no busy-waiting, and every consumer exits cleanly once all work has been processed. Which design meets all three?

options.label: An ArrayBlockingQueue with put and take; the producer enqueues one poison-pill per consumer at the end, and each consumer exits on receiving one
An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue where consumers poll() in a loop with Thread.sleep(10) and quit when they find the queue empty
An ArrayBlockingQueue with put and take; the producer enqueues a single poison-pill, and the consumer that receives it exits
A ConcurrentLinkedQueue with consumers spinning on isEmpty() until the producer sets a volatile done flag

rubric: A bounded blocking queue gives backpressure and no spinning; one poison-pill per consumer ensures every consumer terminates.
A single pill leaves two consumers blocked forever; the other designs are unbounded or busy-wait.

items.prompt: Design a Shape model with exactly Circle, Square and Rect. Every `switch` over shapes must fail to compile if a new variant is later added and not handled, and no default branch is allowed. Which design does this?

options.label: A sealed interface Shape permitting three records, consumed by switch expressions with no default branch
An abstract class Shape with public subclasses, and each switch ending in a default branch that throws IllegalStateException
A plain interface Shape implemented by three classes, with each consumer using instanceof checks and a final else that throws
A Shape class with an enum ShapeType field, and consumers using if-else chains over that field value

rubric: Sealed hierarchies let the compiler check switch exhaustiveness, so a new permitted type breaks unhandled switches at compile time.
The other designs only detect a missing variant at runtime, if at all.

items.prompt: A `TreeSet<Person>` must order by age then name and keep two different people of the same age. The current comparator `(a, b) -> a.age() - b.age()` silently drops people. Which replacement meets all constraints?

options.label: `Comparator.comparing(Person::name)`
`Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age).thenComparing(Person::name)`
`(a, b) -> (a.age() - b.age()) * 100 + a.name().compareTo(b.name())`

rubric: Chaining age then name gives a consistent total order that distinguishes same-age people.
The arithmetic mix breaks ordering, the ternary never returns 0 and violates the Comparator contract, and name-only ignores age.

items.prompt: Your class must be genuinely immutable and holds a `Date` and a `List<String>` passed in by callers. Which changes are needed to meet that goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Mark the fields volatile so changes made by callers are published safely to other threads
Copy the Date and the list in the constructor, and return copies or unmodifiable views from accessors
Synchronize every getter so that readers always see consistent values of the fields
Declare the class final, or make its constructors private, so subclasses cannot add mutable state
Declare all fields private and final, and provide no setters or other mutating methods

rubric: Immutability needs no subclass mutation, private final fields, and defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs.
Volatile and synchronized address visibility or races, not the exposure of mutable state.

items.prompt: A batch job must make 1,000 blocking calls to a rate-limited database. Constraints: at most 20 calls in flight, results returned in input order, and one task's failure must not stop the others. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: Use `Executors.newCachedThreadPool()` and submit every task, since the pool reuses idle threads and so keeps concurrency low
Use `list.parallelStream().map(this::call)` and rely on the common pool's default size staying close to 20 threads
Use `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20)`, submit Callables keeping Futures in input order, and handle ExecutionException per `get()`
Use `Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()` and submit the tasks one after another, so input order is preserved by design

rubric: A fixed pool of 20 caps concurrency, ordered Futures preserve input order, and per-Future exception handling isolates failures.
A cached pool is unbounded, the common pool size is not tied to the limit, and a single thread breaks the throughput goal.
